title: Payday Super – super guarantee paid with each pay run
whoItAffects: All employers with employees (any business paying wages + super)
penalty: Superannuation Guarantee Charge (additional SG shortfall + nominal interest) plus new administrative penalties for late/non-payment; directors' safe harbour lost if Payday Super breached
whatToDo: Move payroll so SG contributions are paid at the same time as wages (or within 7 days) and hit the fund within 7 business days from 1 July 2026.
summary: The Treasury Laws Amendment (Payday Superannuation) Act 2025 requires super guarantee contributions to be paid every pay cycle instead of quarterly. Funds must receive contributions within 7 business days of the payday. Late payments now attract SGC liabilities and administrative penalties from the ATO.

title: $20,000 instant asset write-off made permanent
whoItAffects: Small businesses with aggregated turnover under $10 million
penalty: N/A (concession; incorrect claims risk ATO shortfall penalties)
whatToDo: For eligible assets costing under $20,000, claim an immediate deduction in the year of use (first installed/first used) instead of depreciating.
summary: After years of last-minute extensions, the $20,000 instant asset write-off is now permanent from 1 July 2026 under the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Act 2026. It applies to assets under $20,000 for businesses with aggregated turnover under $10 million.

title: CGT discount replaced with indexation + 30% minimum tax
whoItAffects: Individuals, trusts and partnerships selling assets — including SME owners selling the business or investment assets
penalty: Higher tax on real capital gains (30% minimum tax on gains accruing from 1 July 2027)
whatToDo: Get a valuation and tax advice before 30 June 2027 on the timing of any business or investment asset sale.
summary: The 50% CGT discount for individuals, trusts and partnerships is legislated to be replaced with cost base indexation and a 30% minimum tax rate on capital gains for CGT events on or after 1 July 2027 (Schedule 1, Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Act 2026). Small business concessions and start-up carve-outs were announced 18 June 2026.

title: Negative gearing / residential property tax changes
whoItAffects: SME owners holding residential investment property (established residential properties acquired from 7:30pm AEST 12 May 2026)
penalty: Restricted deductions apply from the 2027–28 income year
whatToDo: Model the after-tax return of any residential investment purchase made after 12 May 2026 before 1 July 2027.
summary: Changes to negative gearing and related housing tax measures for established residential properties acquired from budget night 2026 apply from the 2027–28 income year (1 July 2027), as part of the Tax Reform No. 1 package. Existing holdings are grandfathered.

title: Ban on non-compete clauses (and restrictions on non-solicitation/wage-fixing)
whoItAffects: Employers using post-employment restraints with workers earning under the Fair Work high-income threshold (~$183,100)
penalty: Expected significant civil penalties under the Competition and Consumer Act (final amounts unlegislated)
whatToDo: Audit employment contracts now and replace non-competes with narrower, lawful restraints before the ban commences in 2027.
summary: Treasury consulted in 2025 and released exposure-draft legislation in 2026 to ban non-compete clauses for most workers from 2027, operating prospectively. Non-solicitation and wage-fixing agreement restrictions are also proposed. Final bill passage and exact commencement are still pending.

title: AML/CTF Tranche 2 – lawyers, accountants, real estate, conveyancers, TCSPs
whoItAffects: Law firms, accountants, real estate agents, conveyancers, precious metals/stone dealers, trust & company service providers (mostly small businesses)
penalty: AUSTRAC civil penalties up to tens of millions (currently up to $33M+ per serious contravention) for AML/CTF breaches
whatToDo: If you provide designated services, enrol with AUSTRAC (opened 31 March 2026; enrol within 28 days) and implement an AML/CTF program, KYC and reporting.
summary: Tranche 2 reforms extend AML/CTF reporting-entity obligations to around 100,000 additional businesses from 1 July 2026. Enrolment opened 31 March 2026 and entities providing designated services from 1 July 2026 must enrol within 28 days. Full AML/CTF programs, customer due diligence and suspicious-matter reporting apply.

title: Privacy Act – expanded small business coverage from 1 July 2026
whoItAffects: Small businesses (turnover under $3M) in newly covered categories, incl. businesses trading in personal information and specified service categories (~100,000+ businesses)
penalty: Serious interferences: up to the greater of $50M, 3x benefit, or 30% of adjusted turnover (for larger entities); court-ordered compensation for individuals
whatToDo: If you fall in a covered category, adopt a privacy policy, APP-compliant practices and a data breach response plan from 1 July 2026.
summary: Amendments already in force from 1 July 2026 bring a large new group of small businesses inside the Privacy Act even though the blanket $3M exemption still stands for most. This is the lead-in to the full reform tranche.

title: Privacy Act reform tranche 2 (incl. removal of the small business exemption)
whoItAffects: All businesses with turnover under $3M currently exempt
penalty: Same civil penalty regime as above would apply to formerly exempt small businesses
whatToDo: Monitor the tranche 2 bill and begin basic privacy hygiene (policy, breach plan, data minimisation) ahead of losing the exemption.
summary: The Government has agreed in principle to remove the small business exemption for turnover under $3 million, but the tranche 2 bill tabled in 2026 does not yet do this. The Attorney-General confirmed the reform is progressing; timing is expected around 2027.

title: Scams Prevention Framework – mandatory codes for banks, telcos, digital platforms
whoItAffects: Banks, telecommunications providers and digital platforms and their regulated service suppliers; AFCA membership obligation from 1 Sep 2026
penalty: Civil penalties up to $50 million per contravention; AFCA EDR and private right of action
whatToDo: If you operate a designated financial/telecom/platform service, map your systems against the draft code obligations before 31 March 2027.
summary: The Scams Prevention Framework Act passed in 2024, with designation instruments effective 2025-26. AFCA became the authorised EDR for scam complaints from 1 July 2026 and AFCA-membership obligations bite from 1 September 2026. Substantive code obligations (governance, prevent, detect, disrupt, respond) commence by at least 31 March 2027.

title: Mandatory climate reporting – Group 2 entities (AASB S2)
whoItAffects: Companies meeting two of: revenue ≥$200M, assets ≥$500M, employees ≥250 (near many upper-mid SMEs; also drives supplier data requests)
penalty: Corporations Act civil penalties for misleading sustainability statements and disclosure failures; assurance required from first reporting period
whatToDo: If Group 2-sized, set up FY2026-27 climate data collection; if a supplier, prepare to answer large customers' emissions questionnaires.
summary: Mandatory sustainability reporting under AASB S2 began for Group 2 entities for financial years starting on or after 1 July 2026 (Group 3 follows from 1 July 2027). Even small suppliers are being pulled in indirectly by Group 1/2 customers seeking value-chain emissions data.

title: Mandatory ransomware payment reporting (Cyber Security Act 2024)
whoItAffects: Businesses with turnover over $3M and critical infrastructure asset holders making cyber extortion payments
penalty: Civil penalties up to 60 penalty units (~$19,800 individuals / ~$99,000 body corporate) for failing to report within 72 hours
whatToDo: Add a 72-hour ASD ransomware-reporting step to your incident response plan.
summary: Under Part 3 of the Cyber Security Act 2024, reporting business entities must notify ASD within 72 hours of making (or becoming aware of) a ransomware or cyber extortion payment. There is no minimum payment threshold. The regime has been in force since May 2025.

title: Annual Wage Review 2026 – minimum and award wage increases
whoItAffects: All employers paying award minimums or the national minimum wage
penalty: FWO civil penalties and back-pay for underpayment; intentional underpayment is a criminal offence since 1 Jan 2025
whatToDo: Update payroll for the 4.75% award increases (and higher national minimum wage) from the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026.
summary: The Fair Work Commission's Annual Wage Review 2026 decision raised modern award minimum wages by 4.75% and the national minimum wage by around 6% (to ~$1,004.90/week), effective 1 July 2026. C13/C14 classification structural adjustments also apply.

title: Right to disconnect + casual employee choice pathway (small business)
whoItAffects: Employers with fewer than 15 employees
penalty: FWO civil penalties / FWC dispute orders for breaches of the right to disconnect or failure to respond to conversion notices
whatToDo: Review after-hours contact expectations in contracts and have a documented process for handling casual conversion notices.
summary: From 26 August 2025, employees of small businesses (under 15 staff) gained the right to refuse unreasonable out-of-hours contact, and eligible casuals can use the employee-choice pathway to convert to permanent. Modern awards contain right-to-disconnect terms. These now apply to all employers.

title: Criminal offence for intentional underpayment of wages
whoItAffects: All employers (underpayment of award/entitled amounts)
penalty: Criminal: up to 10 years imprisonment and/or fines up to ~3x the underpayment or $18.78M+ (whichever greater); civil penalties also apply
whatToDo: Run a payroll self-audit against award and NES entitlements; voluntary disclosure and prompt remediation reduce penalty exposure.
summary: Since 1 January 2025, intentionally underpaying employees is a criminal offence under the Fair Work Act, with large fines and imprisonment available. The FWO has a cooperative pathway for genuine mistakes voluntarily disclosed. This remains the dominant compliance risk for SME employers through 2026-27.

title: Commonwealth penalty unit increase $330 → $364
whoItAffects: Any business or individual subject to Commonwealth laws with penalty-unit fines (Fair Work, ASIC, tax, consumer law, privacy, etc.)
penalty: All unit-based fines increased ~10% (e.g. base 60-unit breach now $21,840 instead of $19,800)
whatToDo: Refresh compliance risk numbers — every Commonwealth fine on your register just went up ~10% from 1 July 2026.
summary: The Commonwealth penalty unit value rose from $330 to $364 effective 1 July 2026, mechanically increasing every penalty calculated in penalty units across federal legislation. This flows through to Fair Work, ASIC, OAIC, ACCC and tax administrative penalties.

title: Working Australians Tax Offset (WAUTO)
whoItAffects: Australian workers including sole traders
penalty: N/A (tax concession)
whatToDo: Track the enabling legislation and claim the offset via your 2027–28 tax return once law.
summary: The 2026-27 Budget announced a new $250 annual tax offset for Australian workers, including sole traders, applying from the 2027-28 income year. Enabling legislation is part of the tax reform package before Parliament.

title: Treasury Laws Amendment (Business Registries Stabilisation and Uplift) Bill 2026
whoItAffects: All companies and registered businesses interacting with ASIC registers (fees, registry integrity)
penalty: Registry-related contravention penalties per the Bill; ASIC fee changes
whatToDo: Monitor the Bill's passage and budget for ASIC registry fee/levy changes in 2027.
summary: This 2026 Bill implements stabilisation and funding ('user pays') reforms for the ASIC business registries following the registry failures. Passage will affect annual review fees, lodgement costs and registry integrity obligations for companies.

title: eInvoicing uplift – federal agencies 30% target / Business eInvoicing Right
whoItAffects: Government suppliers and B2B trading partners
penalty: None currently (B2B eInvoicing remains voluntary)
whatToDo: Connect to the Peppol network via your accounting software to keep winning government work and reduce invoice processing costs.
summary: The Government set interim targets for federal agencies to process at least 30% of invoices via eInvoicing (Peppol) by 1 July 2026 and automate sending by December 2026, backed by the Business eInvoicing Right initiative. B2B eInvoicing is not yet mandatory but is being pushed as the practical default for suppliers.

title: Payday Super first-year compliance approach – ATO draft PCG 2025/D5
whoItAffects: All employers during the first Payday Super year
penalty: Risk categorisation (low/medium/high) drives penalty treatment for Payday Super errors
whatToDo: Keep clear evidence of contribution timelines and quickly self-correct errors — ATO's draft PCG scores responsiveness in year one.
summary: The ATO's draft Practical Compliance Guideline PCG 2025/D5 sets out how employers will be risk-rated (low, medium, high) for the first year of Payday Super based on payment behaviour and responsiveness to errors. Finalisation is expected during 2026-27.

title: Casual employment information statement / small business Fair Work statements
whoItAffects: All employers (must give CEIS to new casuals; fair work information statements on hiring)
penalty: Civil penalties for failing to give the statements
whatToDo: Automate issuing the Fair Work Information Statement and Casual Employee Information Statement to every new hire.
summary: Following the Closing Loopholes amendments, employers must give the Casual Employment Information Statement (updated for the employee-choice pathway) to casuals at engagement and at specified intervals. Keep templates current through 2026-27 as award terms update.

title: Statutory review / implementation consultation – CGT reform small business & start-up carve-outs
whoItAffects: SME owners selling businesses; founders and ESOP/start-up investors; testamentary trusts
penalty: Higher CGT from 1 July 2027 unless carve-outs preserve the discount
whatToDo: Lodge or track Treasury submissions on the 18 June 2026 carve-out detail and plan exit timing before 1 July 2027.
summary: On 18 June 2026 the Government released implementation detail for small business, start-up and testamentary trust carve-outs from the CGT discount replacement. Treasury consultation on the carve-outs continues ahead of the 1 July 2027 start; final rules may soften the reform for SME sellers.

title: Unfair contract terms regime – small business protection (ongoing enforcement)
whoItAffects: Any business using standard-form contracts with small businesses or consumers (turnover < $10M counterpart)
penalty: Up to the greater of $50M, 3x benefit, or 30% of adjusted turnover for proposing/relying on unfair terms
whatToDo: Re-audit standard terms (payment clauses, liability caps, unilateral variation rights) against the UCT regime — ASIC/ACCC enforcement is escalating through 2026.
summary: Since November 2023 it is illegal to propose, apply or rely on unfair terms in standard-form small business and consumer contracts. The regime applies to contracts entered or renewed after 10 Nov 2023. Regulators' enforcement intensity against SME-facing contracts continues through 2026-27.

title: Payment Times Reporting Scheme reforms implemented
whoItAffects: Large businesses ($100M+ revenue) reporting payment practices; benefits SME suppliers
penalty: Civil penalties for missed/incorrect six-monthly reports
whatToDo: If a reporting entity, keep six-monthly PTRS reports current; if an SME supplier, use the public data to pressure slow payers.
summary: The Government's 2024-25 reforms to the Payment Times Reporting Scheme are largely implemented per the Regulator's January 2026 update. Large businesses and government enterprises must report payment terms each six months, with data visible to small business suppliers.

title: NewAccess for Small Business – mental health support continuation
whoItAffects: Small business owners and sole traders
penalty: N/A
whatToDo: Refer stressed owner-operators to the free NewAccess for Small Business coaching program, extended with $8M from 1 July 2026.
summary: The 2026-27 Budget provided an additional $8 million from 1 July 2026 to continue NewAccess for Small Business, the free mental health coaching program for small business owners. It is not a compliance item but a usable Commonwealth support.

title: NSW payroll tax annual reconciliation (annual return)
whoItAffects: All NSW payroll tax registered employers
penalty: Interest (PBI) + penalty tax up to 50% on shortfall for late lodgment
whatToDo: Lodge the annual return and pay any balance in Payroll Tax Online by 28 July each year.
summary: NSW employers must reconcile wages paid for the prior financial year against monthly estimates and pay any shortfall. The 2026 return was due 28 July 2026; it recurs every year. Many SMEs miss it because monthly returns continue seamlessly.

title: Victoria payroll tax annual reconciliation
whoItAffects: All Victorian payroll tax registered employers
penalty: General interest charge + penalty tax (up to 75% in dishonest cases)
whatToDo: Complete the annual reconciliation in SRO Online by 21 July, paying any balance or claiming refunds.
summary: Victoria requires annual reconciliation of wages and payment of any balance by 21 July each year (21 July 2026 for FY2025-26). It is a different date to NSW/SA (28 July), catching multi-state employers out.

title: ACT payroll tax: new bands and lower threshold
whoItAffects: ACT employers with Australia-wide wages above $1.75m
penalty: Penalty tax up to 50% + interest on underpaid tax
whatToDo: Re-check your ACT payroll tax rate and threshold from 1 July 2026, especially if grouped or interstate.
summary: From 1 July 2026 the ACT cut its threshold to $1.75m and replaced the flat 6.75% rate with five marginal bands (6.4%-6.85%). Large groups with Australia-wide wages over $150m have been subject to a flat 8.75% rate since 1 January 2026.

title: NT payroll tax 6.5% top rate for very large groups
whoItAffects: Groups with national wages above $100m employing in the NT
penalty: Penalty tax up to 100% for intentional underpayment + interest
whatToDo: If your group exceeds $100m national wages, apply the new 6.5% rate to NT taxable wages from FY2026-27.
summary: From 1 July 2026 the NT added a 6.5% top marginal rate on the portion of wages above $100m national (Australia-wide) wages. The NT general rate (5.5%) and $2.5m threshold are unchanged for most SMEs.

title: QLD Mental Health Levy
whoItAffects: Queensland employers (or groups) with Australia-wide wages over $10m
date: monthly with QLD payroll tax return; annual reconciliation 21 Jul
penalty: Penalty tax up to 75% (intentional) + interest
whatToDo: If your Australia-wide wages exceed $10m, lodge the mental health levy with your payroll tax returns monthly.
summary: Queensland's mental health levy applies to large employers with national wages over $10m ($5m+ for metering enterprises), charged alongside payroll tax. It is collected monthly and reconciled with the annual return due 21 July.

title: QLD apprentice/trainee payroll tax rebate extended
whoItAffects: QLD employers paying apprentices or trainees
penalty: N/A (rebate)
whatToDo: Claim the rebate on apprentice/trainee wages in your QLD payroll tax returns through 30 June 2027.
summary: Queensland extended its 50% payroll tax rebate on apprenticeship and trainee wages to 30 June 2027. Employers claim it in monthly/annual payroll tax returns rather than as a separate application.

title: WA payroll tax annual reconciliation
regulator: Department of Energy, Mines, Industry Regulation and Safety (RevenueWA)
whoItAffects: WA payroll tax registered employers
penalty: Interest + penalty up to 50%
whatToDo: Lodge the WA annual reconciliation and pay any balance by 21 July each year.
summary: WA employers must lodge an annual reconciliation of taxable wages by 21 July following each financial year. Grouped employers must reconcile as a group.

title: SA payroll tax annual return
whoItAffects: SA payroll tax registered employers
penalty: Interest + penalty tax up to 50%
whatToDo: Lodge the SA annual return by 28 July, including interstate wages details.
summary: South Australia's payroll tax annual return is due 28 July each year (28 July 2026 for FY2025-26). SA's threshold is $1.5m with rates up to 4.95%.

title: TAS payroll tax rate bands and annual return
whoItAffects: Tasmanian employers with Australia-wide wages over $1.25m
penalty: Interest + penalty up to 50%
whatToDo: Apply Tasmania's tiered rates (4%-6.1% depending on national wages) and lodge the annual return by 21 July.
summary: Tasmania taxes payroll at tiered rates that increase with Australia-wide wages (4% base up to 6.1% for groups over $100m). The annual return is due 21 July. Wages over $125m attract an additional surcharge.

title: NSW workers compensation reforms (claims/eligibility changes)
whoItAffects: NSW employers and injured workers
penalty: Failure to hold workers comp policy: fines and back premiums
whatToDo: Review updated NSW workers comp claim processes and confirm your policy covers all workers before renewals.
summary: Further amendments to NSW workers compensation legislation commenced on 1 July 2026, changing claim handling and dispute pathways. Employers must hold current icare (or self/agent) cover and adjust to new claim requirements.

title: NSW WHS Code of Practice compliance becomes legally enforceable (s26A)
whoItAffects: All NSW PCBUs (employers/businesses)
penalty: Failure to follow an approved code can be used as evidence in prosecution; WHS Act maximums up to $3.9m/individual, $19.5m/body corporate for Category 1
whatToDo: Audit your systems against NSW approved codes of practice (especially psychosocial hazards) and document compliance or equal-or-better alternatives.
summary: Section 26A of the WHS Act 2011 (NSW) commenced 1 July 2026, making approved codes of practice directly binding: you must comply or show you manage hazards to an equal or better standard. It has major implications for managing psychosocial risks.

title: Victoria retail leasing disclosure statement changes
whoItAffects: Retail landlords (and tenant-facing agents) in Victoria
penalty: Breach of retail leasing disclosure obligations; tenant termination rights for false/incomplete disclosure
whatToDo: Update your s42/50 disclosure statements to the new required format for all new retail leases and renewals.
summary: From 1 July 2026 retail landlords in Victoria must use updated leasing disclosure information under the Retail Leases Act. Tenants can rely on defective disclosure to terminate in some cases, so landlords should review templates.

title: Victoria child employment licensing regime
whoItAffects: Any Victorian business employing children under 15 (incl. entertainment, retail, hospitality)
date: ongoing (licence required; existing permits valid to expiry)
penalty: Up to $223,000 (approx. 1,000+ penalty units) and/or imprisonment for unlicensed child employment
whatToDo: Apply for a child employment licence before employing under-15s, and keep compliant hours/breaks records.
summary: Victoria's reformed Child Employment Act requires a licence (not just a permit) to employ children under 15, with risk-based conditions enforced by the Wage Inspectorate. Existing permits remain valid until expiry.

title: Queensland smoking product (tobacco/vape) supplier licence annual renewal
whoItAffects: QLD retailers, wholesalers and importers of tobacco and vaping products
penalty: Up to ~$370,000 (retail) for selling without a licence; operating without renewal voids authorisation
whatToDo: Renew your smoking product supplier licence before expiry and verify staff hold required authorisations.
summary: Since 1 September 2024 Queensland requires all tobacco and vaping product businesses to hold a licence, renewed annually with fees indexed each financial year. Trading without a current licence attracts six-figure penalties.

title: QLD payroll tax annual reconciliation
whoItAffects: QLD payroll tax registered employers
penalty: Interest + penalty tax up to 50%
whatToDo: Lodge the QLD annual reconciliation by 21 July and claim the apprentice/trainee rebate if eligible.
summary: Queensland annual reconciliations are due 21 July each year. Combined with the mental health levy (for larger employers) and extended apprentice rebates, SMEs should reconcile payroll data early.

title: BAS quarterly lodgment and payment (self-lodgers)
regulator: ATO (applies nationally; listed for all jurisdictions)
whoItAffects: All GST-registered businesses
penalty: Failure to lodge on time (FTL) penalty $330 per 28-day block (5x for large/medium entities) + GIC
whatToDo: Lodge and pay each BAS by the 28th of the month following the quarter (or via agent extended dates).
summary: Quarterly BAS due dates recur as 28 Jul, 28 Oct, 28 Feb and 28 Apr for self-lodgers. Tax agents generally get later agent-due dates. Missing BAS is the most common SME compliance failure.

title: Super guarantee quarterly payment deadline
whoItAffects: All employers with employees
penalty: SG charge (shortfall + 10% admin + nominal interest), non-deductible; from FY2026-27 payable payday (from 1 Jul 2026) with quarterly SMSF deadlines ending 28 Jul / 28 Oct / 28 Feb / 28 Apr
whatToDo: Pay super quarterly by the 28th after each quarter-end; from 1 July 2026 pay super at the same time as wages under payday super.
summary: From 1 July 2026 employers must pay super concurrently with wages (payday super), with quarterly cut-offs for payment to funds by the 28th of the month following each quarter-end. Late super is non-deductible and attracts the SG charge.

title: Payroll tax annual reconciliations across jurisdictions
whoItAffects: Employers registered for payroll tax in any state/territory
date: 21 Jul (VIC, QLD, WA, NT, TAS) / 28 Jul (NSW, SA)
penalty: Interest + penalty tax per jurisdiction
whatToDo: Diary both 21 July and 28 July for payroll tax annual returns if you operate in multiple jurisdictions.
summary: Payroll tax annual reconciliation dates differ: 21 July for VIC, QLD, WA, NT and TAS; 28 July for NSW and SA. ACT follows a 21 July cycle. Multi-state SMEs frequently lodge for one state but miss the other.

title: FBT return and payment
whoItAffects: Employers providing fringe benefits (cars, entertainment, loans)
penalty: FTL penalties + GIC; FBT rate 47%
whatToDo: Collate benefit records for the FBT year ended 31 March and lodge the return by 21 May (or agent's 25 June).
summary: The FBT year ends 31 March; returns are due 21 May for self-lodgers or 25 June via a registered agent (for 2027: 21/25 May-June 2027). SMEs offering cars, EVs or entertainment often overlook FBT entirely.

title: ASIC annual review / solvency resolution for companies
whoItAffects: All proprietary and public companies
date: annually on review date anniversary (+28 days for lodgment, +1 month for payment)
penalty: Late fee $90-$391 per review period; company can be deregistered for non-payment
whatToDo: Within 28 days of your annual review date, pass the solvency resolution and lodge the ASIC annual statement; pay the fee within a month.
summary: Every company receives an annual review from ASIC on its review date. Directors must pass a solvency resolution within 28 days and the review fee must be paid within a month or late fees apply and deregistration can follow.

title: Food safety standard 3.2.2A (food safety supervisor + records)
regulator: QLD Health / local councils (applies in all jurisdictions with state variations)
whoItAffects: Businesses serving food (cafes, restaurants, caterers, childcare)
date: ongoing; food business licence renewals annually with local council
penalty: Council on-the-spot fines (e.g. QLD ~$748-$7,500 per breach) to prosecution
whatToDo: Confirm a current food safety supervisor certificate and required receipt/temperature records before your next council inspection or licence renewal.
summary: Standard 3.2.2A requires most food businesses to have a qualified food safety supervisor and keep key food-handling records. Food business licences with local councils renew annually, and state/council enforcement continues through 2026-27.

title: Victoria food premises registration/classification renewal
whoItAffects: All Victorian food businesses
date: annual (typically 31 Dec or on council registration cycle)
penalty: Trading unregistered: fines up to ~$20,000+ and closure orders
whatToDo: Renew food premises registration with your council and confirm risk classification (Class 1-4) is current.
summary: Victorian food businesses must renew registration with their local council annually under the Food Act 1984, with council risk classifications determining inspection frequency. Renewal lapses are a common, easily-avoided breach.

title: Workers compensation policy renewal
whoItAffects: All employers with workers (incl. contractors deemed workers)
date: annually on policy expiry (most 30 Jun or 1 Oct cycles); wages declarations due at renewal
penalty: Operating uninsured: fines up to ~$66,000 (NSW) / $55,000+ (other states) and back premiums
whatToDo: Declare actual wages and renew the policy before expiry, adding newly deemed workers.
summary: Workers comp policies renew annually (commonly 30 June or 1 October depending on insurer/jurisdiction) and require wage declarations. Trading without cover attracts heavy fines and personal exposure to injury costs. WA specifics: declarations to WorkCover WA insurers each renewal.

title: SA public holidays / retail trading and casual award reform oversight
regulator: Consumer and Business Services (CBS) South Australia
whoItAffects: SA retail and hospitality businesses
penalty: Trading outside authorised hours: fines up to $20,000 (SA Shop Trading Act)
whatToDo: Check CBS retail trading authorisations before opening on restricted public holidays (e.g. Christmas/ANZAC Day).
summary: SA restricts retail trading on major public holidays; shops trading outside exemptions face penalties. CBS also administers several licensing regimes renewing annually. Verify current trading hour authorisations for 2026-27 holiday periods.

title: TAS payroll tax and annual return (21 July)
whoItAffects: Tasmanian employers over the $1.25m threshold
penalty: Interest + penalty up to 50%
whatToDo: Lodge the TAS annual return by 21 July and keep monthly returns current by the 7th of each month.
summary: Tasmanian employers lodge monthly returns by the 7th and reconcile annually by 21 July. Tiered rates (4%-6.1%) depend on Australia-wide wages, so interstate growth can silently push you into higher bands.

title: ACT workers compensation premium and annual wage declaration
whoItAffects: All ACT employers
date: annually at policy renewal (30 Jun cycle common)
penalty: Uninsured employers: fines up to ~$220,000 (ACT) and back premiums
whatToDo: Declare actual wages at renewal (30 June cycle) and confirm the new ACT payroll tax bands are reflected in wage costs.
summary: ACT employers must hold workers comp insurance and declare wages annually at renewal. With the ACT's changed payroll tax bands from 1 July 2026, wage-declaration accuracy matters for both premiums and payroll tax.

title: NT tobacco/vape licensing and business licence renewals
regulator: NT Department of Health / NTG licensing
whoItAffects: NT businesses selling tobacco, vaping products or holding NT business licences
penalty: Selling without licence: fines up to ~$150,000+ (varies by licence type)
whatToDo: Check all NT business licences on the NTG licensing portal and renew before expiry, especially tobacco/vape licences.
summary: NT requires licences for tobacco/vape retail and many commercial activities, renewed annually with indexed fees. Businesses should run a licence stocktake on the NTG portal each year.

title: WHS incident notification and psychosocial duty enforcement (harmonised states)
regulator: WorkSafe WA / Safe Work Australia (model WHS jurisdictions)
whoItAffects: All employers in model WHS jurisdictions (WA, QLD, SA, TAS, NT, ACT, NSW, VIC)
penalty: Category 1 breach up to $3.9m/$19.5m; WA regime similar
whatToDo: Maintain incident reporting procedures and psychosocial hazard controls; notify serious incidents to the regulator immediately.
summary: Model WHS duties on psychosocial hazards are now enforced across all Australian jurisdictions. Notifiable incidents (serious injury, dangerous incidents) must be reported immediately, and regulators (e.g. SafeWork NSW from 1 July 2026) can use codes of practice as direct evidence of breach.

title: NSW Health Records and Information Privacy Act amendments (health records)
whoItAffects: NSW private sector health service providers (clinics, allied health)
penalty: IPC determinations, orders; administrative fines for serious contraventions (verify current amounts)
whatToDo: Review health-information collection notices, access processes and breach procedures against the amended HRIP Act.
summary: NSW's Health Records and Information Privacy Act 2002 received amendment provisions assented 10 June 2026, tightening obligations for private health providers handling health information. NSW private health providers must comply with both state and federal privacy law.

title: QLD notifiable data breach scheme (OIC) for state-held/contracted entities
regulator: Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC) Queensland
whoItAffects: QLD businesses contracting to Queensland Government (contracted service providers) and entities in the MNDB scheme
penalty: OIC compliance notices; federal NDB penalties up to $50m for serious privacy breaches (OAIC)
whatToDo: Implement a notifiable data breach register and response policy covering state and federal scheme obligations.
summary: From 1 July 2026 Queensland's mandatory notification of data breach (MNDB) scheme applies to entities holding QLD government information, including contracted providers, requiring breach registers, policies and notifications to OIC and affected individuals.
